raw_response:
I am a 55-year-old woman who has been farming this land for 30 years. My husband works part-time at a factory in town, so most days it is just me in the fields. We have 10.1 mu of good flat land here in Quzhou, and I have managed wheat-maize double cropping on every single mu for more than two decades. I finished senior high school and later attended some agricultural extension training courses, so I understand soil fertility better than many in my village. But understanding and affording are two different things — with only two of us and limited cash, I have to be careful.

**Winter wheat** was planted last October, mid-month, with Jimai 22 — a reliable improved variety I have used for years. The stand looks uniform this spring. For the base fertilizer at planting, I applied 50 jin (25 kg) per mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) and about 20 jin (10 kg) of urea. That gave me roughly 12 kg of nitrogen per mu in the ground before winter. Now, as the wheat greens up, I need to decide on the spring topdressing. Looking at the wheat color and the soil moisture, I will apply one more topdressing at jointing — about 30 jin (15 kg) of urea per mu, which adds another 7 kg of nitrogen. Total nitrogen for wheat will be around 19 kg per mu. I know some neighbors push 25 kg or more, but my soil tests from two years ago showed medium-high fertility, and honestly, I cannot afford to waste fertilizer. The phosphorus and potassium from the compound fertilizer are enough — about 7.5 kg each per mu. I will irrigate three times this spring: once at green-up in early March, once at jointing, and once at heading if the weather turns dry. Each irrigation costs me about 25 yuan per mu for pumping, so that is a real expense I have to budget for. I sprayed herbicide in early spring when the wheat was at the three-leaf stage, and I am watching for powdery mildew — if it shows up at heading, I will spray fungicide. Harvest will be around June 10.

**Summer maize** comes right after wheat, and the window is brutal — sometimes only five or six days. I will hire a combine for wheat harvest and immediately plant the maize with a no-till planter. I save my own seed sometimes, but for maize I buy hybrid seed every year — Zhengdan 958 is my usual choice, about 70 yuan per mu. At planting, I put down 40 jin (20 kg) per mu of compound fertilizer (15-15-15), and then at the big trumpet stage (around late July) I topdress with 25 jin (12.5 kg) of urea and another 25 jin of compound fertilizer. That gives me about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu for the maize, plus 6 kg each of phosphorus and potassium. I will irrigate twice: once right after planting if the soil is too dry, and once at tasseling-silking in late July or early August — that second irrigation is non-negotiable if I want good kernels. Pre-emergence herbicide is my standard; I cannot spend days hand-weeding with just me and my husband. I expect wheat to give me about 480 kg per mu and maize about 520 kg per mu, assuming no disaster. Last year I got 460 and 510, so I am being slightly optimistic because the winter snow was good.

Labor is tight. For wheat, I handle most management myself — maybe 8 family days total including the spring work. For maize, the planting window is so narrow that I will hire 3 days of labor to help with planting and one day for harvest. Every yuan counts. Total input cost this year will be roughly 6,800 yuan for both crops. That is a lot for us, but skimping on the jointing fertilizer or the silking irrigation would cost me far more in lost yield.
